title: Degree of an Array
description: Brute force to optimized: rebuilding frequency counts per candidate window versus a single-pass first/last/count tracking approach.

blocks.text: Given a non-empty array of non-negative integers nums, the DEGREE of the array is defined as the maximum frequency of any element in it. Return the length of the shortest contiguous subarray of nums that has the same degree as nums itself.

blocks.caption: Track the first index, last index, and count of every value in a single pass

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","A non-empty array of non-negative integers nums"],["Output","The length of the shortest contiguous subarray whose degree equals the degree of the whole array"],["Goal","Find this in a single linear pass, without checking every possible subarray individually"],["Constraints","1 <= nums.length <= 5 * 10^4; 0 <= nums[i] <= 5 * 10^4"]]}

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["The degree is the MAXIMUM frequency of any single value","Only the values achieving this maximum frequency ever matter for the answer"],["A qualifying subarray must contain every occurrence of some max-frequency value","Its shortest possible span for that value is exactly (last occurrence index - first occurrence index + 1)"],["Multiple values could tie for the maximum frequency","Compute this span for every value reaching the degree, and take the minimum"]]}

blocks.text: Given nums, first find its degree (the highest frequency of any element), then find the length of the shortest contiguous subarray that still has that same degree.

blocks.title: Analogy: The Tightest Fence Around a Popular Landmark
blocks.text: Like knowing which landmark (a repeated value) appears most often across a row of towns, and wanting to build the shortest possible fence that still encloses every single appearance of that landmark. The fence must start no later than the landmark's first appearance and end no earlier than its last, so the tightest possible fence spans exactly from the first to the last occurrence.

blocks.caption: For each value reaching the degree, its tightest span is last occurrence minus first occurrence plus one

Value 2: first index 1, last index 2, span 2","Spans: 5 and 2","Only values achieving the degree need their span checked"],["Answer","2","The value 2's span of 2 is shorter than value 1's span of 5"]]}

Degree = 3","Degree: 3","The value 2 alone achieves the highest frequency here"],["Value 2: first index 1, last index 6, span 6","Span: 6","This is the tightest possible span covering all three occurrences of 2"],["Answer","6","Only value 2 reaches the degree, so its span is the answer directly"]]}

blocks.text: Before checking every possible subarray's degree directly, notice that a qualifying subarray is entirely determined by whichever value it's built around.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The degree of the whole array is simply the maximum frequency among all its values, easily found with a single frequency count.

Observation 2: A subarray achieves this same degree only if it fully contains every occurrence of at least one value that reaches that frequency in the original array (a shorter subarray could never contain all of that value's occurrences, and thus couldn't match its count).

Observation 3: For any single value, the SHORTEST possible subarray containing all of its occurrences is exactly the span from its first occurrence to its last occurrence, inclusive.

Observation 4: Track the first index, last index, and total count of every distinct value in a single pass, then take the minimum span among only the values whose count equals the degree.

Recognizing that the answer only depends on the extremes (first/last occurrence) of degree-reaching values collapses an apparently expensive subarray search into a single-pass tracking problem.

This is a single-pass tracking pattern: maintain running first-seen and last-seen indices (alongside a frequency count) for every distinct value, then derive the answer directly from that tracked information.
First compute the degree directly, then check every possible subarray to find the shortest one matching that degree.

items: Compute the frequency of every value in nums, and take the maximum as the degree.
For every possible starting index, extend forward until the window's own maximum frequency equals the degree, recording the shortest such window found.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The degree is computed once upfront over the full array, since it never changes regardless of which subarray is being tested.
A fresh count map is built for every starting position, since each candidate window's local frequencies must be tracked independently.
The inner loop breaks as soon as a window matching the degree is found, since any longer window from that same start could never be shorter.

blocks.text: Every possible subarray is checked directly against the target degree, so the correct minimum length is always found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared) in the worst case, since each of the n starting positions can extend forward and rebuild its count map up to n times.
Space: O(n) for the count maps.

Limitation: rebuilding a frequency count for every candidate window ignores that the answer only ever depends on the first and last occurrence indices of the handful of values that reach the array's degree, which can be tracked directly in a single pass.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force rebuilds a frequency count for every candidate window. Instead, make a single pass over nums, tracking three things per distinct value: the index of its first occurrence, the index of its most recent (last) occurrence so far, and its running count. After this single pass, the degree is simply the maximum count seen, and the answer is the minimum span (last - first + 1) among only the values whose count equals that degree.

In one pass, update first[x] only the first time value x is seen, always update last[x] to the current index, and increment count[x]. Track the running maximum count as the degree. After the pass, scan every distinct value whose count equals the degree, and return the minimum of (last[x] - first[x] + 1) among them.
Track first-seen index, last-seen index, and count for every value in a single pass, then derive the answer directly.

blocks.title: Deriving the final answer
blocks.text: degree = 2. Values reaching degree 2: value 1 (first=0, last=4, span=5) and value 2 (first=1, last=2, span=2). The minimum span is 2, matching the expected answer.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single pass to build the tracking maps, plus a pass over the distinct values (at most n) to find the minimum span.
Space: O(n) for the three tracking maps.

Any subarray that matches the array's degree must fully contain every occurrence of at least one value that reaches that degree (otherwise, that value's count within the subarray would be strictly lower than its count in the full array, unable to reach the degree). The shortest possible subarray containing all occurrences of a specific value is necessarily bounded by that value's first and last occurrence, so checking only the values that reach the degree, and taking the minimum such span, finds the true answer.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["A value's count equals the degree","Its span (last - first + 1) is a valid candidate answer"],["A value's count is less than the degree","It can never anchor a qualifying subarray, since no subarray containing it could match the full array's degree through this value alone"]]}

items: first[x] is set only once, on the very first encounter of x, using a "set if absent" check.
last[x] is overwritten on every encounter of x, always holding its most recent index by the end of the pass.
degree is tracked as a running maximum during the same single pass that builds the tracking maps, avoiding any second full pass over nums itself.

blocks.text: The key insight is that a qualifying subarray is entirely determined by the first and last occurrence of some degree-reaching value, turning what looks like a subarray search into a simple tracking-and-lookup problem.

items: Checking every value's span, not just those reaching the degree, which can produce an incorrect (too-short) answer from a value that doesn't actually match the array's degree.
Recomputing frequencies for every candidate subarray instead of tracking first/last/count directly in one pass over the original array.
Forgetting to update last[x] on every occurrence (not just checking whether it exists), since it must always reflect the MOST RECENT index seen.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["nums has only 1 element","The degree is 1, and the answer is 1 (the single element itself)"],["Every value in nums is distinct","The degree is 1, and the answer is 1, since any single element already matches the degree"],["Multiple values tie for the highest frequency","The shortest span among all of them is the answer"]]}

items: Explicitly justify why the shortest qualifying subarray must always span exactly from a value's first to its last occurrence, since this justification is the key logical step connecting the problem to a simple tracking solution.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Shortest subarray matching some frequency/count property of the full array" points toward tracking first-seen and last-seen indices per value in a single pass, then deriving the answer from those extremes directly.

items: How would you handle this if the array were streamed (values arriving one at a time, unknown length)? The same first/last/count tracking works incrementally; only the final degree-and-minimum-span computation needs to wait until the stream ends (or be recomputed incrementally as new maximums appear).
What if you needed the actual shortest subarray itself, not just its length? Track which value achieves the minimum span, then directly slice nums from that value's first to last occurrence.

How would this change if "degree" were defined as the SECOND-highest frequency instead? The same tracking approach still works, just filtering for values whose count matches the second-highest frequency instead of the maximum.

A single-pass tracking pattern (first-seen / last-seen indices per value), distinct from the running-sum style of classic Kadane's Algorithm, though grouped in the same category for its similarly simple, single-linear-pass structure.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n squared) time, O(n) space.
Optimized (single-pass tracking): O(n) time, O(n) space.

items: Pattern: Single-pass tracking of first-occurrence index, last-occurrence index, and count per distinct value
Core Idea: A qualifying subarray must span from some degree-reaching value's first to its last occurrence; take the minimum such span
Time: O(n)
Space: O(n)
Most Important Observation: The shortest subarray matching the array's degree is always bounded by the first and last occurrence of some value that reaches that degree
Interview Difficulty: Easy
One-line memory trick: Track first/last/count per value; answer is min(last - first + 1) among values at the degree
